title: Simple Problem, Deep Thinking
author: Daniel Golazeski
summary: Former math teacher Daniel Golazeski argues that lessons should begin with a deliberately simple, tangible problem so every student can think, I get it. His example is a geometry segment diagram where the answer, 4 minus 3, is obvious in under a second. Rather than rush on, he pushes students to notice that their brain first saw an addition idea, 3 plus something makes 4, which becomes the Segment Addition Postulate without memorization. When the same idea later appears as a messy algebraic equation, students can translate it into one part plus the other part equals the total. He acknowledges that skipping to the real content is pushed by common lesson plans, pacing and test pressure, but contends that the basics are the real content.
points: Golazeski observes that students who say they hate math usually mean they hate feeling stupid, so early success matters.
He starts lessons with a preposterously simple example and uses it to demand deep thinking about why the answer is true.
Guided questions lead students to see the subtraction as an addition idea, so the postulate is discovered, not memorized.
The simple foundation makes the later algebraic version of the problem easier to translate and solve.
He defends departing from a homogenized common lesson plan when it better serves students than the paperwork does.
quotes: Students who say, “I hate math!” usually mean, “I hate feeling stupid!” This article explores one way to turn our classrooms into a place where students feel smart.
Starting with a simple first example gives all our students the opportunity to think, “I get it!
If we want to help students feel confident, we need to help them feel competent.
A math problem students can answer in less than a second is often a perfect opportunity to demand deep thinking.

Instead of forcing them to memorize “The Segment Addition Postulate says that the total length of a segment is always equal to the sum of its parts,” I get my students to realize they already know this concept.

The trouble with this line of thinking is that the basics are the real content. Expecting students to master a topic without giving them a chance to understand its foundation is a recipe for disaster.
But if we allow what’s good for a school’s paperwork to come before what’s good for our students, we’re teaching for all the wrong reasons.
